In the suit, Atiku had alleged forgery of the National Youth Service Corps discharge certificate.
Atiku had sued Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress (APC) and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
The judge said the time allowed by law to make such presentation of exhibit was within 14 days, being a pre-election suit and in line with section 285(9) of the 1999 Constitution.
Justice Ekwo agreed with Tinubu and other defendants in the suit that, if Atiku is allowed to bring fresh evidence, the character of the initial case would change and would be in breach of the 1999 Constitution.
In his ruling on Friday, on the application by Atiku to amend his originating summons, the court held that Atiku attempted to mislead the jury in his claim that he would not present fresh issue in the amendment sought.
Justice Ekwo said after carefully perusing the application, the Court found that the ADC presidential candidate sought to substitute old evidence for a new one which, if allowed, would over reach the section 285(9) of the Constitution which says such evidence must have been provided within 14 days.
According to the judge, a fundamental injustice would be done to the defendants if Atiku is permitted to bring fresh evidence through the back door against them.
Meanwhile, by consensus agreement of lawyers, the judge has fixed December 2 for the hearing of the substantive matter.
Atiku had told the court that he needed to make substantial amendment to his case challenging the eligibility of Tinubu to participate in the 2027 presidential election.
Atiku and ADC had in the main suit asked Justice Inyang Ekwo to disqualify President Tinubu and APC from the 2027 presidential election.
They had questioned Tinubu’s National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) by APC.
The plaintiffs, who sued the president, APC and INEC as 1st to 3rd defendants in the originating summons marked: FHC/ABJ/CS/1888/2026, alleged that APC submitted the President’s forged NYSC discharge certificate to INEC.
They, therefore, prayed the court to compel INEC to remove Tinubu and APC’s names from the list of candidates and parties for the presidential poll.
But President Tinubu and APC, in their joint counter affidavit filed on September 9, prayed the court to dismiss the suit in its entirety for being incompetent and that the plaintiffs lacked the legal right to institute the case.
They denied submitting any forged certificate to INEC either for the 2023 or 2027 presidential elections.
INEC, in its preliminary objection filed on September 7 by its lawyer, Dr Alex Izinyon (SAN), also challenged the competence of the suit on the grounds of statute-bar, want of locus standi, absence of a reasonable cause of action and abuse of court process.
The commission argued that the plaintiffs failed to comply with the mandatory written deposition requirement under Paragraph 7(1) provision of the Federal High Court Pre-Election Practice Directions (Amendment) 2026.
Atiku and ADC, however, approached the court with a motion on notice on September 10, seeking an amendment to the suit.
